item.title: Empty Responses at the Token Cap: reading done_reason=length in an Ollama agent loop (2026)
item.description: A tool-calling turn can return HTTP 200 with empty content and no tool_calls: the token cap fired mid-call. Read done_reason=length, and why raising the cap did not help here.
item.content:encoded:
An agent sends a request with a tools array and a modest output cap. The server answers HTTP 200, the body parses, and the assistant message is empty: content is "", tool_calls is absent, and no error field explains it. The loop logs “model returned no content”, retries the identical request, and the next turn is empty in the same way. The operator starts suspecting the model, the quantisation or the chat template, because nothing in the client raised an exception.

The response already contains the diagnosis. Read the stop reason and the token count before anything else: done_reason is "length" on the native /api/chat surface, finish_reason is "length" through /v1/chat/completions, and eval_count (native) or usage.completion_tokens (compatible surface) equals the cap that was set. The cap fired while the model was still emitting its tool-call preamble. In the chat handler a parsed call is emitted when the parser closes it: it is attached to the streaming chunk that completed it, or to the aggregated non-streaming response once generation is over. A call still incomplete when generation ends is never emitted at all, because the final chunk carries only whatever text the parser was holding outside the call. So the partial call is dropped rather than returned, and the response looks like an ordinary completed turn with nothing in it.

That is the whole diagnostic, and it fits in one response. The rest of this article is the fixture that produced it, the server code path behind it, and a negative result that matters for the obvious fix: on this fixture, raising the cap from 8 to 64 tokens did not restore the call.

The fields that separate a truncated call from a finished turn

Both surfaces expose the same state with different names. The native handler returns done_reason and eval_count; the OpenAI-compatible handler maps max_tokens onto the same internal cap and returns finish_reason plus usage. The tools documentation for Ollama v0.20.3 shows the normal shapes of a streamed and a final /api/chat response, and the OpenAI-compatibility page lists max_tokens and tools as supported parameters.

What to read Native POST /api/chat POST /v1/chat/completions
why generation stopped done_reason choices[0].finish_reason
tokens actually generated eval_count usage.completion_tokens
call present message.tool_calls message.tool_calls
the limit you set options.num_predict max_tokens

Three combinations are worth memorising, because they lead to different actions:

  • length plus a token count equal to your cap: the cap fired. Any partial call was dropped. This is the case measured here.
  • stop with a non-empty content and no tool_calls: the model answered in prose instead of calling a tool. Raising the cap will not change that.
  • tool_calls present: a call was parsed and returned. Whatever goes wrong after this is argument or client-side validation, not truncation.

The num_predict option is documented in the v0.20.3 Modelfile reference as the maximum number of tokens to predict, defaulting to -1 for unbounded generation. The cap in a failing request is therefore the caller’s own number, not a hidden model limit.

What the measured run shows

The fixture is deliberately small and boring: qwen2.5:0.5b (Q4_K_M, 397 MB, 4096-token context) on Ollama 0.20.3, one create_ticket tool schema with three required fields (title, priority as an enum, summary), temperature 0, seed 7. Two prompt variants were used: A with a long operator preamble and a detailed customer message, B with a one-sentence preamble and a short request. Caps of 8, 16, 24, 32, 40 and 48 tokens were requested on both variants and both API surfaces, five repetitions per cell, with one extra repetition in the native variant-A cell at cap 24 and one further cell at 64 on the native surface. The run recorded 129 requests in total. The table below counts every request per cap, so its rows already include the two native streaming cells at caps 16 and 48; the remaining 127 requests are the graded cells.

Cap Requests Empty content, no tool_calls Complete calls Stop reason
8 20 20 0 length
16 21 21 0 length
24 21 21 0 length
32 20 20 0 length
40 20 20 0 length
48 21 21 0 length
64 5 5 0 length
96 1 0 1 stop

Every request at caps 8 through 64 returned HTTP 200 with content of length zero, no tool_calls, and a stop reason of length. On the native surface eval_count equalled the cap in every one of those requests; on the compatible surface usage.completion_tokens equalled max_tokens in all 60 compatible requests. The empty message is not a client serialisation artefact: the same state appears in the raw JSON body, on both surfaces, with the token accounting that proves generation happened.

The single exception in the log is one request at 96 tokens on the native surface with variant A: a complete create_ticket call, done_reason "stop", eval_count 95. It is one observation, not a boundary. No repetition was made at 96, variant B was not tested there, and the compatible surface never reached a complete call inside the tested range. Treat it as evidence that the fixture can complete at a larger cap, not as a value to copy.

Why the content is empty rather than truncated

The intuitive model of a token cap is “the answer gets cut off”, and for plain text that is what happens: you receive a partial sentence. With a tools array the observable is different, because a partial tool call has nowhere to go in the response schema.

In the chat handler of server/routes.go at v0.20.3, the branch that runs when the request carries a tools array hands each chunk to the tool parser (toolCalls, content := toolParser.Add(res.Message.Content), line 2493). When the parser closes a call, that branch attaches the calls to the chunk that completed them and empties the content (res.Message.ToolCalls = toolCalls; res.Message.Content = "", lines 2496-2501). When it has not closed one, the final chunk carries whatever text the parser is still holding and nothing else - if r.Done { res.Message.Content = toolParser.Content(); ch <- res }, lines 2513-2515 - and a non-streaming call then attaches the collected calls only when at least one closed call was parsed: if len(toolCalls) > 0 { resp.Message.ToolCalls = toolCalls }, lines 2608-2610. A generation stopped at the cap still reports done, but an unterminated call never becomes an entry in that slice, so the attachment is skipped and the message goes out with empty content. (The older /api/generate path applies the same rule in GenerateHandler with a different field, if cr.Done && len(toolCalls) > 0 { res.ToolCalls = toolCalls } at lines 584-585; every measurement in this article is on the chat path, where /api/chat and the /v1/chat/completions wrapper are both served by ChatHandler.) The response that reaches the client is a normal completion carrying an empty content string and no tool_calls. Nothing in that payload is marked as an error, because from the server’s point of view nothing failed: the client’s limit was honoured exactly.

The compatible layer inherits the same shape. In openai/openai.go at v0.20.3, max_tokens is copied into the internal num_predict option, and for a non-streaming response the finish reason is rewritten to tool_calls only when the response actually carries tool calls; otherwise the underlying done_reason string is returned unchanged. Streaming applies the same rule in toChunk, which reports tool_calls when the chunk itself carries calls or when an earlier chunk already sent one (toolCallSent), so the rewrite tracks calls having been emitted rather than calls present in the final message alone. A dropped partial call therefore keeps finish_reason: "length" instead of being rewritten into something a client might notice.

This is why the failure is so quiet in an agent loop. A text-generation client that checks only for empty content can treat the turn as a no-op; a tool-calling client that checks only for tool_calls sees “no call” and often assumes the model chose not to act. The stop reason is the field that separates those cases, and it is present in every response.

The negative result: raising the cap did not fix it on this fixture

The obvious remedy is to raise the limit. On this fixture it did not work over an eightfold range. Twenty graded runs at 48 tokens - five per cell across the two prompt variants and the two surfaces - plus the one streaming request at that cap produced zero complete calls, and five runs at 64 on the native surface also produced zero. The first and only complete call in the log came at 96 tokens, in a single run.

Two readings of that result are tempting and both are wrong. The first is that 96 is the required cap; with n=1 and one variant it supports no such constant, and the same schema on another model or template will spend a different number of tokens before the call closes. The second is that the cap value is irrelevant, which over-reads a single model. What the run does establish is narrower and still useful: the empty state is stable from 8 to 64 tokens, so a retry loop that bumps the cap by a small increment will keep producing identical empty turns while burning time, and a diagnostic that relies on “it will work with a bigger number” has no measured basis here.

The practical consequence is to stop treating the cap as the variable to tune and treat the empty response as the signal to inspect. If the stop reason is length, the request needs a different shape - a shorter preamble, a smaller schema, or a generation budget sized to the template - not the same request submitted again with a larger number.

A check you can run on one response

The detection step needs no server logs and no framework instrumentation. Take the response object your client already has, pass in the cap you sent, and check the three fields together:

def capped_without_call(resp, cap, native=True):
    """cap is the limit you sent, not a field the server echoes back."""
    if native:
        reason, tokens = resp.get("done_reason"), resp.get("eval_count")
        message = resp.get("message") or {}
    else:
        choice = (resp.get("choices") or [{}])[0]
        reason, tokens = choice.get("finish_reason"), (resp.get("usage") or {}).get("completion_tokens")
        message = choice.get("message") or {}
    return (reason == "length"
            and not message.get("content")
            and not message.get("tool_calls")
            and cap is not None and tokens == cap)

cap is an argument because the response does not carry it. In api/types.go at v0.20.3, ChatResponse (line 534 onward) has no options field - Options is declared on ChatRequest (line 168) - and the compatible body exposes usage.completion_tokens but never max_tokens, so the limit has to come from the request you sent and be compared against the token count the server reports. Pass the num_predict value you set, or the max_tokens you passed to the wrapper; the two are the same number after the mapping described above.

The predicate is a reading aid, not a fix: it tells you that the cap fired and the call was dropped. Log done_reason, eval_count and the configured cap on every turn, not only on errors, so the state is visible the first time it happens rather than after a retry storm. When the predicate is true, do not resubmit the identical request; change the prompt or the budget first, or surface the state to the operator.

Two neighbours are worth reading alongside this one. The Ollama API integration guide covers the request and response fields this article relies on, and the function-calling guide explains finish_reason as the signal for detecting a call; this piece is the case where that signal reads length instead. For the prompt-side failure that looks similar but is not the same, the context-truncation diagnosis covers a prompt that is cut before generation starts, and the concurrent-session logging checklist already names length plus num_predict as the stop signal for text turns, though not for a discarded tool call. Readers running the same loop against a different engine can compare the parser behaviour in the vLLM streaming tool-call case, and the local agent guide covers the retry structure in which one empty turn becomes a stall.

Fixture, reproduction and limits

The run used two stdlib urllib scripts against the local daemon at 127.0.0.1:11434, no SDK. Each request recorded the HTTP status, wall time, content length, presence of tool_calls, JSON-parseability of the arguments and whether every required key was present, plus done_reason/finish_reason and eval_count/usage.completion_tokens. The graded table, the raw request log, the environment capture and the method note are kept with the draft as a private local author verification; they are not offered here as a downloadable dataset or a reusable harness, so no reader-access promise is made for those files. The fixture is described completely enough to rebuild: one model tag, one tool schema, two prompts, one sampling setting, and the caps listed above.

The limits are the honest part of this result. It is one host (2 vCPU, recorded load average 4.64 before the sweep and 3.47 and 2.73 at two in-run checkpoints), one model, one quantisation, one tool schema, two prompt variants, and 129 requests. Requests went to a shared local daemon rather than a dedicated server instance, so wall times are provenance only and no throughput or latency claim is drawn from them. The single 96-token completion is one run on one variant, and no boundary is asserted across variants or surfaces. Nothing here measures how often this happens across models, and no prevalence figure is implied. What is supported is the diagnostic: a length stop with a token count equal to the cap and an empty message is the signature of a capped generation whose partial tool call was discarded, and on this fixture raising the cap across an eightfold range did not restore the call.

item.title: Ollama's Silent Tool-Call Failures: Conversation-History Round-Trip, Dropped Calls and Retyped Arguments
item.description: Four open Ollama reports: tool calls vanish or come back retyped — empty turns with done_reason stop, an integer returned as "30000.0", prose-only replies.
item.content:encoded:
An agent loop calls a local Ollama server, the HTTP status is 200, the stream ends cleanly, and the assistant message contains nothing: no content, no tool_calls, done_reason: "stop". The loop treats that as “the model is done” and stops. Nothing was done. No error was raised.

That is the failure this article is about. It is not one bug with one cause. Four separate, currently open reports against Ollama between versions 0.34.1 and 0.40.8 describe four different ways a tool call disappears or comes back mutated, and the source of tag v0.40.12 shows which of those paths are still present in the newest release at the time of writing.

The evidence boundary matters, so state it up front: four public issue reports written by other people, plus reads of the tagged source. No Ollama server was started for this article, so nothing here is a benchmark, and nothing here is our own reproduction. Where a number is quoted, it is the reporter’s own count on their own harness, at the version they named.

The signature to recognise before anything else

A dropped tool call and a genuinely finished turn look identical in most clients, because both are done_reason: "stop" with an assistant message. The distinguishing field is eval_count. A dropped call still generated tokens: the model wrote a call, the server failed to return it as tool_calls, and the tokens are counted. The reporter on qwen3:8b saw eval_count between 20 and 160 on replies whose content and tool_calls were both empty.

So the operational rule is narrow and testable: an assistant turn with empty content, no tool_calls, done_reason of stop and a non-zero eval_count is a server-side loss, not a completed task. A turn with eval_count: 0 may genuinely be empty output. Most agent frameworks collapse both into “finished” and move on.

The rest of this article is the four paths that produce the first case, then the guard.

The four paths in one table

Path Trigger Wire symptom Server signal Reported on
History retyping An integer argument from an earlier tool call is replayed through history Next call returns the argument as the string "30000.0", client schema validation rejects it, and keeps rejecting it none 0.40.8, flint:40b-a2b-qat-int4
Unregistered tool Model calls a function name that is not in the request’s tools array content empty, tool_calls absent, eval_count above zero none 0.40.7 (also 0.40.4/0.40.5), qwen3:8b; 0.40.8, qwen3:0.6b
Unclosed list in arguments gemma4 leaves the edits list unclosed in a tool call Empty assistant turn, no error field gemma4 tool call parsing failed 0.40.6 (Windows/CUDA), gemma4:e4b
Preamble before the call System prompt asks for prose, then a call Prose only, tool_calls: null, done_reason: stop none 0.34.1, qwen3.8:27b-mlx

Two of the four are parser or renderer defects. One is a type loss in the API decode that only becomes visible through a renderer. One is a model- and build-specific suppression that has not been shown to exist on newer versions. Treating them as a single “Ollama drops tool calls” defect would be wrong, and the scope of each is the reason the fixes are tracked as separate pull requests.

Path 1: history replay retypes an integer

The first report (issue #19191) is precise enough to read as a specification. With flint:40b-a2b-qat-int4 on Ollama 0.40.8 (f580b54), a request whose history contains an earlier tool call carrying timeout_ms: 30000 returns the next call with {"command":"pwd","timeout_ms":"30000.0"}. Without that earlier call in history, the same model returns proper integers on nine of nine runs; with it, the wrong form appears on three of three.

Two layers produce that, and separating them matters if you are deciding what to patch.

The decode layer loses the integer type before any model sees the prompt. In api/types.go at tag v0.40.12, ToolCallFunctionArguments.UnmarshalJSON rebuilds the arguments with json.Unmarshal into an ordered map, which decodes every JSON number as float64. Message.UnmarshalJSON wraps its alias type, so this path runs for every history message that carries tool calls. This is type loss, not value loss: float64 holds integers exactly far beyond any plausible timeout value, but the fact that the value was an integer is gone by the time a renderer formats it.

The render layer decides whether the type loss becomes visible text. In model/renderers/flint_json.go at the same tag, flintJSONValue handles floats itself: it formats with strconv.FormatFloat(..., 'g', -1, ...), appends .0 whenever the result contains no ., e or E, and returns the string as a json.Number, so a float64 of 30000 is turned into the literal 30000.0 before the shared writer sees it. flint.go sends every non-string tool-call argument through that conversion on the way into <arg_value>, which is how 30000 becomes <arg_value>30000.0</arg_value> in the Flint prompt. Flint then copies the form it was shown, and returns it as a string.

That .0 is this renderer’s, not a rule of Ollama’s JSON handling in general. pythonScalar in model/renderers/json.go at the same tag re-reads the marshalled value with UseNumber and returns a number literal that contains no ., e or E unchanged; only a literal that does contain one is parsed to float64, formatted with 'f', and given a trailing .0 when that result has no dot. A raw float64 of 30000 marshals to 30000 and comes out as 30000 there.

The downstream damage is durable rather than transient. Once a call carrying the string form is appended to history, every later call that sets the same argument is rendered from the same mutated history and fails the same validation, so an agent that survived turn two dies on turn three and stays dead for the session. The reporter’s client rejected it with invalid type: string "30000.0", expected u64, and their shell tool could not run any command for the rest of the session.

Both halves are addressed in open pull requests, neither merged into v0.40.12: api: preserve integer types in decoded tool call arguments (PR #19195) switches the decode to preserve number representation, and Fix tool calls rendering integer arguments as decimals (PR #19252) stops the renderer from rewriting the numeric form. If your client validates argument types, check your server version against both before assuming a fix is present.

Path 2: the call names a tool that is not in tools

The second path is the one that most often hides inside a working agent, because the trigger is a design pattern people adopt deliberately: a tool offered on demand, named inside another tool’s description, rather than listed in the request’s tools array.

The report is issue #19187. On Ollama 0.40.7 with qwen3:8b, /api/chat streaming, num_ctx 32768, a call to such a name returned no content and no tool_calls, with eval_count between 20 and 160. Replaying sixteen captured requests, the reporter got that empty reply on 28 of 32 runs. Generating raw text for the same requests with the model’s own template produced a well-formed <tool_call> to the unlisted name every time, and adding the missing names to tools with empty schemas restored the call on 30 of 32. The model was calling; the server was dropping the call on the way out.

An independent reporter reproduced it on 0.40.8 (Linux, CPU) with qwen3:0.6b, and their counts are cleaner: with the target tool absent from tools, eight of eight seeds returned no content and no tool_calls with eval_count 25; with it listed, eight of eight returned the call. They saw the same empty reply through /v1/chat/completions, with finish_reason stop, so switching endpoints does not route around it.

The mechanism proposed in PR #19240 is that the parser buffers a tagged call for a name it does not recognise, and the content accessor returns an empty string for non-JSON tags, so the API emits a successful response with neither content nor tool calls. That is the contributor’s account, not a path confirmed by reading v0.40.12, so treat it as the best available explanation rather than a verified one. The PR is open.

The practical consequence: if your agent exposes tools dynamically by mentioning them in a description, the request that “should” work will silently produce nothing, and the retry loop will keep producing nothing. Listing the tool, even with an empty parameter schema, is the difference between 28 of 32 empty and 30 of 32 working.

Path 3: the repair closes braces, never brackets

The third path is in gemma4 argument parsing (issue #19273), and it is the clearest case of a one-line log message that looks harmless. The reporter’s build is Ollama 0.40.6 on Windows with CUDA, and they note that model/parsers/gemma4.go has not changed since commit a9d8953 (2026-09-22), so their observation extends to 0.40.11.

A gemma4 call that leaves the edits list unclosed still ends with its closing tag, so the model finished the call. The parser’s repair candidates close a string delimiter, and they add a missing } only when another repair already changed the text. At v0.40.12, in model/parsers/gemma4.go, the object-close repair returns immediately when the argument text already ends in }, and no repair step inserts a ] at all. So a call of the shape call:edit{edits:[{newText:S,oldText:S,path:S} has nothing in the repair path that can rescue it. The parser logs gemma4 tool call parsing failed and returns a reply with no content, no tool_calls, done_reason: "stop", and no error field.

The reporter’s counts come from five days of agent evals with gemma4:e4b through OpenClaw: 30 dropped edit calls in the server log, every one leaving the edits list unclosed, across 16 failed runs in 28 rounds. Their four observed call shapes split on what is missing — path inside the item with both ] and the outer } absent (20 occurrences), ] missing before ,path (5), ] and outer } missing (4), and one case with two items where only the ] was missing. Those are one reporter’s task mix, not a benchmark, but the shape distribution is the useful part: a single missing bracket, not a mangled call.

PR #19274 adds a repair that closes the lists a finished gemma4 call leaves open. It is open. Until it lands, a gemma4 agent should treat the log line gemma4 tool call parsing failed as an incident marker and re-ask, not as noise.

Path 4: the announce-then-call pattern on an MLX build

The fourth path is the narrowest and the one most likely to be a version artifact, so it is stated with its environment attached.

The report is issue #19353. On qwen3.8:27b-mlx with Ollama 0.34.1 (macOS 26.5.2, Apple M4 Pro, 48 GB, qwen3_5 architecture, nvfp4), a system prompt that asks the model to say something in natural language before calling the tool produces prose only: tool_calls is null and done_reason is stop. The same request with a tool-directive prompt returns parsed calls, and a control model, qwen3:4b, returns finish_reason: tool_calls with a non-empty preamble on three of four runs of the identical prompt. Only the system prompt differs between the two cases.

This is the shape of an announce-then-call instruction, which is a common agent pattern, so the report matters even though the version does not overlap the 0.40.x series. What it does not support is any claim about v0.40.12. Nothing here shows the behaviour reproduced on a newer build, and no source shows it fixed. If you run a preamble-style prompt on an MLX build, check this first; if you run it on a current CPU or CUDA build, you have no evidence either way from this report.

The guard: an empty turn is an error, not a completion

Everything above is detectable client-side without patching the server, because the failure is a specific shape on the wire rather than an exception. The whole check is small enough to paste into the response handler:

def lost_tool_call(msg, done_reason, eval_count):
    return (done_reason == "stop"
            and not (msg.get("content") or "").strip()
            and not msg.get("tool_calls")
            and (eval_count or 0) > 0)

When that predicate is true, treat the turn as a transport-level failure for the loop’s purposes: do not append it to history as an assistant completion, do not fall through to a final answer, and either re-ask with the tool registered in tools or surface an error to the caller. Appending the empty message is the specific mistake that turns a recoverable drop into a session-ending stop, because the next request then replays a history in which the model appears to have said nothing.

Three supporting behaviours make the guard usable in practice:

  • Log done_reason and eval_count on every turn, not only on errors. Without eval_count you cannot tell a dropped call from a genuinely empty reply, and you will spend the debugging session on the model.
  • Validate argument types against the tool schema on the way in, before you append a call to history. The integer-to-string mutation survives forever once replayed, so the cheapest place to catch it is the moment it arrives.
  • Before concluding a fix is missing or present, read the server version and compare it with the open pull requests listed above. The v0.40.12 release was published on 2026-10-27T00:07:12Z, and none of the four pull requests referenced here is merged into it.

Where to look first when a turn comes back empty

Order the checks by cost, cheapest first, and stop at the first one that explains the observation:

  1. History serialisation. Does the request you sent contain the argument types you intended, or did a previous response already hand you "30000.0"? If the latter, the server-side retype happened one turn earlier.
  2. The tools array. Is every function name the model could plausibly call actually listed, including the ones you only mention inside descriptions?
  3. The server log. One line, gemma4 tool call parsing failed, names the parser path outright; its absence does not clear the other paths, which log nothing.
  4. The model and build. Preamble suppression and MLX render paths are model- and build-specific, and are the last thing to blame, not the first.

For the surrounding mechanics, the Ollama API integration guide covers the /api/chat request shape these probes use, and the gemma4 setup guide covers installation and the errors that are not tool-call related. If a model looks worse rather than silent, why a local LLM feels dumber covers quantisation, context and sampling — a different failure class from state corruption.

What this article does not claim

It does not claim that all Ollama parsers or renderers share one defect: each of the four paths is reported against one model-parser or model-renderer pair, and the code observations are specific files at one tag. It does not claim the paths were reproduced here; no server was run. It does not claim the reports are current for v0.40.12 in either direction — none of them shows the behaviour on that tag, and none of the four pull requests is merged. The counts quoted, including 28 of 32, 30 of 32, eight of eight, three of three, 30 dropped calls and 16 of 28 runs, are the reporters’ own on their own harnesses, at the versions they named, and are not normalised for hardware. No search-volume, keyword or traffic figure is claimed anywhere; the demand signal for this topic was repository issue incidence, which measures reported pain, not query volume.

The source records, fetched page bodies and code files behind this article are a private local author check kept beside the draft, not a downloadable dataset: the issue and pull-request payloads are third-party content, and republishing them is not something this article does. Every claim above links to the public page it came from, and those pages are the record to open.
